blocks.p: When the time came and the court was in session, Mr. True-man, the jailer, was ordered to bring the prisoners down to the bar. So they were brought down, their arms bound and chained together, as the custom of the town of Mansoul was. When they had been presented before the Lord Mayor, the Recorder, and the rest of the honorable bench, the jury was sworn in first, and then the witnesses. The names of the jury were these: Mr. Belief, Mr. True-heart, Mr. Upright, Mr. Hate-bad, Mr. Love-God, Mr. See-truth, Mr. Heavenly-mind, Mr. Moderate, Mr. Thankful, Mr. Good-work, Mr. Zeal-for-God, and Mr. Humble.
The names of the witnesses were Mr. Know-them-all, Mr. Tell-true, and Mr. Hate-lies, with my Lord Willbewill and his man, if they were needed.
So the prisoners were set at the bar. Then Mr. Do-right, who was the Town Clerk, said, “Set Atheism at the bar, jailer.”
So he was set at the bar.

“Atheism, raise your hand,” said the Clerk. “You are indicted here by the name of Atheism, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having wickedly and stupidly taught and maintained that there is no God, and therefore no attention need be paid to religion. This you have done against the being, honor, and glory of the King, and against the peace and safety of the town of Mansoul. What do you say? Are you guilty of this indictment, or not?”
“Not guilty,” said Atheism.
“Call Mr. Know-them-all, Mr. Tell-true, and Mr. Hate-lies into the court,” cried the Crier.
So they were called, and they appeared.
Then the Clerk said, “You witnesses for the King, look at the prisoner at the bar. Do you know him?”
“Yes, my lord, we know him,” said Mr. Know-them-all. “His name is Atheism. He has been a poisonous fellow in the miserable town of Mansoul for many years.”
“You are sure you know him?”
“Know him! Yes, my lord. I have been in his company far too often to be ignorant of him now. He is a Diabolonian, the son of a Diabolonian; I knew his grandfather and his father.”

“Well said,” said the Clerk. “He stands indicted by the name of Atheism, and so on, and is charged with teaching that there is no God, and so no attention need be paid to any religion. What do you witnesses for the King say to this? Is he guilty or not?”

“My lord,” said Mr. Know-them-all, “he and I were once in Villain’s Lane together, where he was talking briskly about all sorts of opinions; and then and there I heard him say that, for his part, he believed there was no God. ‘But,’ he said, ‘I can profess one, and be as religious as anybody, if the company I’m in and the circumstances of other things put me up to it.’”
“You are sure you heard him say this?”
“On my oath, I heard him say it.”
“Mr. Tell-true,” said the Clerk, “what do you say to the King’s judges about the prisoner?”
“My lord, I used to be a great companion of his, which I now repent of; and I have often heard him say, and with great defiance, that he believed there was neither God, angel, nor spirit.”
“Where did you hear him say so?”
“In Blackmouth Lane and in Blasphemer’s Row, and in many other places besides.”
“Do you know much about him?”

“I know him to be a Diabolonian, the son of a Diabolonian, and a horrible man for denying God. His father’s name was Never-be-good, and he had more children than this Atheism. I have nothing more to say.”
“Mr. Hate-lies,” said the Clerk, “look at the prisoner at the bar. Do you know him?”

“My lord, this Atheism is one of the vilest wretches I ever came near or had dealings with in my life. I have heard him say that there is no God; I have heard him say there is no world to come, no sin, no punishment hereafter; and more than that, I have heard him say that it was as good to go to a brothel as to go and hear a sermon.”
“Where did you hear him say these things?”
“In Drunkard’s Row, just at Rascal Lane’s End, at a house where Mr. Impiety lived.”

“Set him aside, jailer,” said the Clerk, “and set Mr. Lustings at the bar.” Then he turned to the prisoner. “Mr. Lustings, you are indicted here by the name of Lustings, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having devilishly and treacherously taught, by your practice and your filthy words, that it is lawful and profitable for a man to give way to his bodily desires; and that you for your part have never denied yourself, and never will deny yourself, any sinful pleasure as long as your name is Lustings. What do you say? Are you guilty of this indictment, or not?”

Then Mr. Lustings said, “My lord, I am a man of high birth, and I have been used to the pleasures and pastimes of the great. I am not accustomed to being snubbed for what I do, but have been left to follow my will as if it were law. And it seems strange to me to be called to account today for what not only I, but almost all men, secretly or openly approve, love, and allow.”

“Sir,” said the Clerk, “we are not concerned with your greatness (though the higher you were, the better you should have been). We are concerned, and so are you now, with an indictment brought against you. What do you say? Are you guilty of it, or not?”
“Not guilty.”
“Crier, call on the witnesses to stand forward and give their evidence.”
“Gentlemen, you witnesses for the King,” cried the Crier, “come in and give your evidence for our Lord the King against the prisoner.”
“Come, Mr. Know-them-all,” said the Clerk, “look at the prisoner at the bar. Do you know him?”
“Yes, my lord, I know him.”
“What is his name?”
“His name is Lustings. He was the son of one Beastly, and his mother gave birth to him in Flesh Street; she was the daughter of one Evil-Craving. I knew the whole family of them.”
“Well said. You have heard his indictment. What do you say to it? Is he guilty of the things charged against him, or not?”
“My lord, he has indeed been a great man, as he says; and a thousand times greater in wickedness than in pedigree.”
“But what do you know of his particular actions, especially as to his indictment?”

“I know him to be a swearer, a liar, a Sabbath-breaker; I know him to be a fornicator and an unclean person; I know him to be guilty of a great many evils. To my knowledge he has been a very filthy man.”
“But where did he usually commit his wickedness? In private corners, or more openly and shamelessly?”
“All over town, my lord.”
“Come, Mr. Tell-true, what have you to say for our Lord the King?”
“My lord, all that the first witness has said I know to be true, and a great deal more besides.”
“Mr. Lustings,” said the Clerk, “do you hear what these gentlemen say?”

“I have always been of the opinion,” said Lustings, “that the happiest life a man could live on earth was to hold himself back from nothing he desired in the world. I have never once been false to this opinion of mine, but have lived in love with my notions all my days. And having found such sweetness in them myself, I was never so mean-spirited as to keep the praise of them from others.”
Then the Court said, “Enough has come out of his own mouth to lay him open to condemnation. So set him aside, jailer, and set Mr. Incredulity at the bar.”
Incredulity was set at the bar.

“Mr. Incredulity,” said the Clerk, “you are indicted here by the name of Incredulity, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having feloniously and wickedly, while an officer of the town, led the resistance against the captains of the great King Shaddai when they came and demanded possession of Mansoul. Yes, you defied the name, the forces, and the cause of the King; and you also, as Diabolus your captain did, stirred up and encouraged the town of Mansoul to rise against and resist the said forces of the King. What do you say to this indictment? Are you guilty of it, or not?”

Then Incredulity said, “I do not know Shaddai. I love my old prince. I thought it my duty to be true to my trust, and to do what I could to persuade the men of Mansoul to resist strangers and foreigners to the utmost, and fight them with all their might. Nor have I changed my opinion, nor will I, for fear of trouble, though you hold office and power for now.”

Then the Court said, “The man, as you see, is incorrigible. He means to defend his villainies with bold words, and his rebellion with shameless confidence. So set him aside, jailer, and set Mr. Forget-good at the bar.”
Forget-good was set at the bar.

“Mr. Forget-good,” said the Clerk, “you are indicted here by the name of Forget-good, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having, when all the town’s affairs were in your hands, utterly forgotten to serve them in what was good, and having sided with the tyrant Diabolus against Shaddai the King, against his captains and all his army, to the dishonor of Shaddai, the breaking of his law, and the danger of the destruction of the famous town of Mansoul. What do you say to this indictment? Are you guilty, or not guilty?”

Then Forget-good said, “Gentlemen, now my judges: as to the indictment accusing me before you of several crimes, I beg you to put my forgetfulness down to my age and not to my willfulness, to the feebleness of my brain and not to the carelessness of my mind; and then I hope that by your charity I may be excused from great punishment, even though I am guilty.”

Then the Court said, “Forget-good, Forget-good, your forgetfulness of good was not mere frailty but deliberate, because you hated to keep good things in your mind. What was bad you could hold on to, but what was good you could not bear to think of. So you use your age and your pretended feebleness to blind the court, and as a cloak to cover your knavery. But let us hear what the witnesses say for the King against the prisoner. Is he guilty of this indictment, or not?”
“My lord,” said Mr. Hate-lies, “I have heard this Forget-good say that he could never bear to think of goodness, no, not for a quarter of an hour.”
“Where did you hear him say so?” said the Clerk.
“In All-base Lane, at a house next door to the sign of the Conscience Seared with a Hot Iron.”
“Mr. Know-them-all, what can you say for our Lord the King?”

“My lord, I know this man well. He is a Diabolonian, the son of a Diabolonian; his father’s name was Love-Evil. And as for this man, I have often heard him say that he counted the very thought of goodness the most burdensome thing in the world.”
“Where have you heard him say these words?”
“In Flesh Lane, right across from the church.”
Then the Clerk said, “Come, Mr. Tell-true, give your evidence about the prisoner at the bar, on the matter for which he stands indicted by this honorable Court.”
“My lord, I have often heard him say that he would rather think of the vilest thing than of what is contained in the Holy Scriptures.”
“Where did you hear him say such grievous words?”
“Where? In a great many places; particularly in Nauseous Street, in the house of one Shameless, and in Filth Lane, at the sign of the Reprobate, next door to the Descent into the Pit.”
Then the Court said, “Gentlemen, you have heard the indictment, his plea, and the testimony of the witnesses. Jailer, set Mr. Hard-heart at the bar.”
He was set at the bar.

“Mr. Hard-heart,” said the Clerk, “you are indicted here by the name of Hard-heart, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having most desperately and wickedly filled the town of Mansoul with impenitence and stubbornness, and kept them from remorse and sorrow for their evils all through their falling away from, and rebellion against, the blessed King Shaddai. What do you say to this indictment? Are you guilty, or not guilty?”

“My lord,” said Hard-heart, “I never knew what remorse or sorrow meant in all my life. I am impenetrable. I care for no man; nor can I be pierced by other men’s griefs; their groans will not get into my heart. Whoever I harm, whoever I wrong, it is music to me, when it is mourning to them.”
“You see,” said the Court, “the man is a true Diabolonian, and has convicted himself. Set him aside, jailer, and set Mr. False-peace at the bar.”
False-peace was set at the bar.

“Mr. False-peace, you are indicted here by the name of False-peace, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having most wickedly and satanically brought, held, and kept the town of Mansoul, both in her falling away and in her hellish rebellion, in a false, groundless, and dangerous peace, and a damnable sense of security, to the dishonor of the King, the breaking of his law, and the great damage of the town of Mansoul. What do you say? Are you guilty of this indictment, or not?”

Then Mr. False-peace said, “Gentlemen, and you who are now appointed to be my judges: I acknowledge that my name is Mr. Peace; but that my name is False-peace I utterly deny. If your honors will send for anyone who knows me intimately, or for the midwife who delivered me, or for the godparents who were at my christening, any or all of them will prove that my name is not False-peace but Peace. So I cannot plead to this indictment, since my name is not in it. And as my true name is, so is my character. I was always a man who loved to live in quiet, and what I loved myself, I thought others might love too. So when I saw any of my neighbors laboring under a troubled mind, I helped them as well as I could; and I could give many instances of this good temper of mine, such as these.

“First: when at the beginning our town of Mansoul turned away from the ways of Shaddai, some of them afterward began to have troubling second thoughts about what they had done. But I, distressed to see them so, at once looked for ways to quiet them again.

“Second: when the ways of the old world, and of Sodom, were in fashion, if anything happened to disturb those who kept to the customs of the times, I worked to quiet them again, and to let them go on undisturbed.

“Third, to come nearer home: when the wars broke out between Shaddai and Diabolus, if at any time I saw any of the town of Mansoul afraid of destruction, I often worked, by some means, device, invention, or other, to bring them back to peace. So, since I have always been a man of such a virtuous temper as some say a peacemaker is, and if a peacemaker is as deserving a man as some have been bold enough to claim, then let me, gentlemen, be counted by you, who have a great name in Mansoul for justice and fairness, as a man who deserves not this inhuman treatment, but liberty, and also leave to sue my accusers for damages.”
Then the Clerk said, “Crier, make a proclamation.”

“Oyez!” cried the Crier. “Since the prisoner at the bar has denied that his name is the one in the indictment, the Court requires that anyone here who can inform the Court of the prisoner’s original and true name come forward and give evidence; for the prisoner stands upon his own innocence.”

Then two men came into the court and asked leave to say what they knew of the prisoner. The name of one was Search-truth, and the name of the other Vouch-truth. So the Court asked these men whether they knew the prisoner, and what they could say about him; “for he stands,” they said, “upon his own vindication.”
Then Mr. Search-truth said, “My lord, I—”
“Wait!” said the Court. “Swear him in.”
So they swore him in, and he went on.

“My lord, I know this man, and have known him from a child, and I can testify that his name is False-peace. I know his father; his name was Mr. Flatter. And his mother, before she was married, went by the name of Mrs. Smooth-over. These two, when they came together, did not live long without this son, and when he was born they named him False-peace. I was his playmate, only I was a little older than he was; and when his mother used to call him home from play, she would say, ‘False-peace, False-peace, come home quick, or I’ll come and get you.’ Yes, I knew him when he was still nursing; and though I was very little then, I can remember that when his mother used to sit at the door with him, or play with him in her arms, she would call him twenty times in a row, ‘My little False-peace! My pretty False-peace!’ and ‘Oh, my sweet rascal, False-peace!’ and again, ‘Oh, my little bird, False-peace!’ and ‘How I love my child!’ The women who were at his christening know it is so too, though he has had the nerve to deny it in open court.”
Then Mr. Vouch-truth was called on to say what he knew of him, and they swore him in.

“My lord,” said Mr. Vouch-truth, “all that the previous witness has said is true. His name is False-peace, the son of Mr. Flatter and of Mrs. Smooth-over, his mother. And in former times I have seen him angry with anyone who called him anything but False-peace, for he would say that all such people were mocking him and calling him names. But that was in the days when Mr. False-peace was a great man, and when the Diabolonians were the fine gentlemen of Mansoul.”

Then the Court said, “Gentlemen, you have heard what these two men have sworn against the prisoner at the bar. And now, Mr. False-peace, to you. You have denied that your name is False-peace, yet these honest men have sworn that it is. As for your plea, it is entirely beside the matter of your indictment. You are not charged here with doing evil because you are a man of peace, or a peacemaker among your neighbors, but because you wickedly and satanically brought, kept, and held the town of Mansoul, both in its falling away from its King and in its rebellion against him, in a false, lying, and damnable peace, contrary to the law of Shaddai, and to the danger of the destruction of the then miserable town of Mansoul. All you have pleaded for yourself is that you deny your name, and so on; but here we have witnesses to prove you are the man. As for the peace you boast so much of making among your neighbors, know this: peace that is not the companion of truth and holiness, peace that is without this foundation, is built on a lie, and is both deceitful and damnable, as the great Shaddai himself has said. So your plea has not delivered you from what the indictment charges you with; rather, it fastens it all the more firmly on you. But you shall have entirely fair play. Let us call the witnesses to the facts, and see what they have to say for our Lord the King against the prisoner at the bar.”
“Mr. Know-them-all,” said the Clerk, “what do you say for our Lord the King against the prisoner?”

“My lord, to my knowledge this man has long made it his business to keep the town of Mansoul in a sinful quiet in the midst of all her lewdness, filth, and turmoil. And he has said in my hearing, ‘Come, come, let us run from all trouble, whatever ground it comes from, and let us be for a quiet and peaceable life, even if it has no good foundation.’”
“Come, Mr. Hate-lies, what have you to say?”
“My lord, I have heard him say that peace, even in the way of unrighteousness, is better than trouble with truth.”
“Where did you hear him say this?”
“I heard him say it in Folly Yard, at the house of one Mr. Simple, next door to the sign of the Self-deceiver. Yes, to my knowledge he has said it twenty times in that place.”

“We may spare any further witnesses,” said the Clerk. “This evidence is plain and full. Set him aside, jailer, and set Mr. No-truth at the bar.” Then he turned to the prisoner. “Mr. No-truth, you are indicted here by the name of No-truth, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having always, to the dishonor of Shaddai and the danger of the utter ruin of the famous town of Mansoul, set yourself to deface and utterly destroy all the remains of the law and image of Shaddai that have been found in Mansoul since her deep falling away from her King to Diabolus, the envious tyrant. What do you say? Are you guilty of this indictment, or not?”
“Not guilty, my lord,” said No-truth.
Then the witnesses were called, and Mr. Know-them-all gave evidence first.

“My lord, this man was at the pulling down of the image of Shaddai; yes, he is the one who did it with his own hands. I stood by and saw him do it myself, at the command of Diabolus. Yes, this Mr. No-truth did more than that: he also set up the horned image of the beast Diabolus in the same place. And he is the one who, at the bidding of Diabolus, ripped and tore and had burned up all he could of the remains of the law of the King, whatever he could lay his hands on in Mansoul.”
“Who saw him do this besides you?” said the Clerk.

“I did, my lord,” said Mr. Hate-lies, “and so did many others; for this was not done secretly, or in a corner, but in the open sight of everyone. Yes, he chose to do it publicly, because he delighted in doing it.”
“Mr. No-truth,” said the Clerk, “how could you have the face to plead not guilty, when you were so plainly the doer of all this wickedness?”

“Sir,” said No-truth, “I thought I had to say something, and as my name is, so I speak. It has worked to my advantage before now, and for all I knew, speaking no truth might reap me the same benefit now.”

“Set him aside, jailer,” said the Clerk, “and set Mr. Pitiless at the bar.” Then to the prisoner: “Mr. Pitiless, you are indicted here by the name of Pitiless, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having most treacherously and wickedly shut up every feeling of compassion, and for refusing to let poor Mansoul grieve over her own misery when she had fallen away from her rightful King, but instead evading, and at every turn twisting her mind away from, any thoughts that tended to lead her to repentance. What do you say to this indictment? Guilty or not guilty?”

“Not guilty of pitilessness,” said the prisoner. “All I did was to cheer people up, as my name says; for my name is not Pitiless but Cheer-up, and I could not bear to see Mansoul inclined to melancholy.”
“What!” said the Clerk. “Do you deny your name, and say it is not Pitiless but Cheer-up? Call the witnesses. What do you say to this plea?”

“My lord,” said Mr. Know-them-all, “his name is Pitiless; that is how he has signed himself on every paper of any consequence he has had to do with. But these Diabolonians love to disguise their names. Mr. Covetousness covers himself with the name of Good-Management, or something like it; Mr. Pride, when he needs to, can call himself Mr. Neat, or Mr. Handsome, or the like; and so with all the rest of them.”
“Mr. Tell-true, what do you say?”

“His name is Pitiless, my lord. I have known him from a child, and he has done all the wickedness charged in the indictment. But there is a whole set of them who know nothing of the danger of damnation, and so they call everyone melancholy who thinks seriously about how to escape that state.”

“Set Mr. Haughty at the bar, jailer,” said the Clerk. “Mr. Haughty, you are indicted here by the name of Haughty, an intruder on the town of Mansoul, for having most treacherously and devilishly taught the town of Mansoul to carry itself proudly and defiantly against the summons given to them by the captains of King Shaddai. You also taught the town of Mansoul to speak with contempt and scorn of their great King Shaddai; and moreover you encouraged Mansoul, by both word and example, to take up arms against the King and against his Son Emmanuel. What do you say? Are you guilty of this indictment, or not?”

“Gentlemen,” said Haughty, “I have always been a man of courage and valor. Even under the darkest clouds I have never been one to sneak about, or hang my head like a bulrush; nor did it ever please me to see men take off their hats to those who opposed them, even when their enemies seemed to have ten times the advantage of them. I never stopped to consider who my enemy was, or what the cause was that I was engaged in. It was enough for me if I carried myself bravely, fought like a man, and came off the victor.”

“Mr. Haughty,” said the Court, “you are not indicted for having been a valiant man, nor for your courage and boldness in times of distress, but for having used this pretended valor of yours to draw the town of Mansoul into acts of rebellion against the great King and against Emmanuel his Son. This is the crime, and the thing you are charged with in and by the indictment.”
But he gave no answer to that.
When the Court had proceeded this far against the prisoners, they turned them over to the verdict of the jury, addressing the jury in this way:

“Gentlemen of the jury, you have been here and have seen these men; you have heard their indictments, their pleas, and what the witnesses have testified against them. What remains is for you to withdraw at once to some place where you can consider without confusion what verdict, in truth and righteousness, you ought to bring in for the King against them, and then bring it in.”

Then the jury, that is, Mr. Belief, Mr. True-heart, Mr. Upright, Mr. Hate-bad, Mr. Love-God, Mr. See-truth, Mr. Heavenly-mind, Mr. Moderate, Mr. Thankful, Mr. Humble, Mr. Good-work, and Mr. Zeal-for-God, withdrew to do their work. And when they were shut up by themselves, they began to talk it over in order to draw up their verdict.
Mr. Belief, who was the foreman, began. “Gentlemen,” he said, “as for these men, the prisoners at the bar, for my part I believe they all deserve death.”
“Quite right,” said Mr. True-heart. “I am entirely of your opinion.”
“Oh, what a mercy it is,” said Mr. Hate-bad, “that such villains as these have been caught!”
“Yes, yes!” said Mr. Love-God. “This is one of the most joyful days I ever saw in my life.”
Then Mr. See-truth said, “I know that if we sentence them to death, our verdict will stand before Shaddai himself.”
“Nor do I question it at all,” said Mr. Heavenly-mind; and he added, “When all such beasts as these are cast out of Mansoul, what a fine town it will be then!”

“It is not my way to pass judgment rashly,” said Mr. Moderate. “But their crimes are so notorious, and the evidence so plain, that a man must be willfully blind who says the prisoners ought not to die.”
“Blessed be God,” said Mr. Thankful, “that the traitors are in safe custody.”
“And I join you in that on my bare knees,” said Mr. Humble.
“I am glad too,” said Mr. Good-work.
Then that warm and true-hearted man, Mr. Zeal-for-God, said, “Cut them off. They have been the plague of Mansoul, and have sought her destruction.”
So, all being agreed in their verdict, they came straight into the Court.

“Gentlemen of the jury,” said the Clerk, “answer all to your names. Mr. Belief, one; Mr. True-heart, two; Mr. Upright, three; Mr. Hate-bad, four; Mr. Love-God, five; Mr. See-truth, six; Mr. Heavenly-mind, seven; Mr. Moderate, eight; Mr. Thankful, nine; Mr. Humble, ten; Mr. Good-work, eleven; and Mr. Zeal-for-God, twelve. Good men and true, stand together in your verdict. Are you all agreed?”
“Yes, my lord,” said the jury.
“Who will speak for you?”
“Our foreman.”

“Gentlemen of the jury, sworn in for our Lord the King to serve in a matter of life and death, you have heard the trials of each of these men, the prisoners at the bar. What do you say? Are they guilty of the crime, and the crimes, for which they stand indicted here, or are they not guilty?”
“Guilty, my lord,” said the foreman.
“Look to your prisoners, jailer,” said the Clerk.
This was done in the morning, and in the afternoon they received the sentence of death according to the law.
So the jailer, having received this charge, put them all in the inner prison, to keep them there until the day of execution, which was to be the next morning.
